paragraphs.asr_text: This needle has pointed north your whole life, but the seafloor remembers further back. North and south have swapped, again and again, with no schedule.
That needle follows a field that wraps the whole planet. It feels permanent. It is not.

At ocean ridges, fresh lava cools into rock. Tiny magnetic grains lock in the field's direction. The seafloor spreads, and each flip starts a new stripe. Five million years, about 20 flips, and wildly uneven gaps.
So, two questions. When will it flip next? And how often does it flip? Which one can we answer?
In a simple computer model of a flipping field, the first is hopeless. The second is not.
Finding out why takes us through liquid metal and chaos, then to machines that dream up snapshots of magnetic fields. They must obey some laws exactly, and others only on average.
How often does the field flip? A learner's map of the Milady project, from a compass to today's research.
Should the first simulations target how often the field flips, or the warning signs just before a flip?

Is there a giant magnet hidden inside the Earth? Deep down, the outer core is an ocean of liquid iron. Left alone, a field there would fade away within tens of thousands of years. Yet Earth's field is several billion years old, so the moving iron must keep making it all the time.
Take a bar magnet, north at one end, south at the other. Cut it in half. You get two magnets, each with a north and a south. No one has ever found a lone magnetic pole.
Field lines say the same. They never start or stop. Draw any box and count. As many lines go in as come out. Keep this box in mind.
A bicycle dynamo turns motion into electricity using a built-in magnet. The earth has to make its own. The trick? A loop.
Hold a microphone near its own speaker and turn up the gain. Below a certain point, a whisper fades. Past it, the loop feeds itself.
Now, spin a copper disk wired to a coil around its axle. Current makes field, and field makes current. Spin it faster and faster. Does the field grow bit by bit, or not at all until some speed?

Not at all, until a threshold. Past it, each turn multiplies a tiny seed field by the same factor, exponential growth. Just past the threshold, growth is slow. Then the field breaks the disc, and growth stops.

Who pays for all this? A motor drives the flow. In the earth, convection does. The flow stretches the field. The field breaks the flow. Once growth stops, every watt that goes in leaves as heat, on average. A dynamo turns motion into field. It creates no energy.
Earth's field points one way today. Which way should it prefer?

Reverse every field line. The dynamo's equations read the same. So, neither. The two directions are mirror twins, equally lawful. Which one you get is history, not law. In the disc, the seed's sign decides, and nothing in the laws forbids a flip.
Moving iron. A loop with a threshold. No favorite direction. But the disc had wires. Liquid iron has none. Then what motion can do it? And how fast?
Near the threshold, should dynamo simulations start from a tiny seed, a strong one or both?
What kind of motion can grow a magnetic field? In a perfect conductor, field lines would be threads frozen into the fluid. Wherever the flow stretches a thread, the field along it grows stronger.

Real metals let the threads smudge, like spreading ink. The smudging speed is set by the metal's magnetic diffusivity. Same flow, two metals. A good conductor smudges slowly. The threads stay sharp. A poor one smudges fast. The threads blur away.

One number keeps the score, the magnetic Reynolds number, Rm. It is the flow's speed times its size divided by the magnetic diffusivity. Large Rm, stretching out paces smudging. Small Rm, smudging winds.
Turn the RM knob up and watch a weak seed field. At low RM, the seed dies away. Past a threshold, the growth rate crosses zero and the seed grows like the squeal.

Laboratory dynamos use liquid sodium. It flows as easily as water, but a field smudges in it about 100,000 times faster than its swirls do. Their ratio, 1 in 100,000, is the magnetic prandtl number, PM.
Reaching an RM of a few tens takes violent stirring. The flow's Reynolds number, the gauge of turbulence, reaches millions. So every laboratory dynamo is turbulent.

Only three liquid-sodium experiments have made their own field, each a different kind. In Riga, a corkscrew flow made a field that oscillates and slowly turns. In Karlsruhe, 52 spiraling cells made a steady field, close to a dipole. And only VKS at Katerash made a dipole that can flip.
A fourth, Dressdyne and Dresden aims to join them, a spinning cylinder whose axis slowly turns.
Inside VKS, a cylinder holding 150 liters of liquid sodium. At its ends, two bladed discs, the impellers, spin in opposite directions.
Should it matter what metal the disks are made of?
With stainless steel discs, there was no dynamo, even at full speed. Swap in discs of soft iron and a dipole grows along the axis.
So the threshold depends on more than RM. Materials count too.
Now spin the two discs at different speeds. At some settings, the dipole flips again and again, with no schedule. Like the compass needle at the start, but every minute or two.
Each flip itself takes only about five seconds. Uneven stripes, like the seaflores, but written in minutes, not millions of years.
Simulations cannot reach sodium's tiny PM. Which PM values should the first three-dimensional runs cover?
Riga, Karlsruhe, and VKS crowned a hunt of nearly a century. Here is its map.
Lane 1, the Earth's record. Lava's magnetized backwards, 1906. Seafloor stripes, 1963. Then flips as chance events whose odds change over the ages.
Lane 2. Theory. 1919. A moving, conducting fluid might keep the sun's field alive. 1933. No flow can sustain a field that is symmetric around an axis.
1958, the first proven examples of flows that can. In the 70s came simple dynamo flows, later the blueprints of Riga and Karlsruhe.
Lane 3. Building a dynamo. 1963. A model dynamo of spinning iron cylinders. 1999. Sodium makes its own field. In Riga. Then Karlsruhe.
2006. VKS. Only with iron discs. Then the first flips of a turbulent sodium dynamo.

Lane 4. Computers. 1981. Simulated turbulence grows dynamos. 1995. A simulated Earth's core reverses its field. Ringed pins mark papers cosigned by this project's supervisors. 1997. Two simulated counter-rotating eddies make a dynamo. 2005. Such dynamos still work at a PM of 100th.

From 2016, two codes simulate the VKS tank, iron impellers included. 2026. Both make it flip. In the runs explored only with conducting surroundings, savings, their reference run, a Reynolds number near 1600, not millions.
Lane 5. A few dials instead of a tank. 1958. Two coupled disc dynamos already flip. 2012. Three dials that flip by chaos alone. We will play with them soon.
2026. Four dials fitted to the simulated VKS flips by a method that finds equations and data.

Milady began in 2026, bringing machine learning where tanks, computers, and dials meet. Yet the data-driven lane is thin. In 2022, the learning methods one study tried could not reliably foresee a geomagnetic flip.
The internship and a proposed thesis at a bet. Machines that dream up dynamo fields and obey their physics.
Behind every lane, the same race. Stretching against smudging.
Back to the race. The flow stretches the field, and diffusion smudges it. Physicists write the very same race as a single equation.

On the left, how fast the magnetic field changes at each point. First term on the right, the flow carries the field along and stretches it like the threads. Second term, diffusion smudges it at a pace set by the magnetic diffusivity. A pore conductor smudges fast. Stretching against smudging, the whole race in one line.

Picture the flow as a conveyor belt that does not feel its cargo. A weak field rides on the imposed flow and fades or grows exponentially. On a log scale, a straight line whose slope is the growth rate.
But a strong field pushes back on the flow. As it break the copper disk, the line bends into a plateau. These are the kinematic and dynamic regimes. Flips live on the plateau.
To test ideas, physicists need a flow simple enough to write on one line, yet able to make a dynamo. One classic choice, the ABC flow.
It fills space with identical twisting rooms. Three crossed winds make the fluid corkscrew. It spins around the direction it moves. This box returns higher on our climb.
Now turn one knob on this flow, Rm. Turning it up means less diffusion. Less smudging should only help the stretching.
So once the dynamo switches on, it stays on, right?

Here is the growth rate, computed at 24 settings. Below about nine, every field fades. Then growth turns positive. The dynamo is on. Near 17 and a half, it switches off again. Above about 27, it comes back. Not one threshold, but windows. Turning a knob further does not always help. It agrees with published results. No machine learning yet. This only tests the solver.

Real dynamos have not one knob, but a panel. How hard the metal is stirred. How well it conducts. What the discs are made of. Remember the iron. How unequal their speeds are. That is when VKS flipped. For Dresden, a precessing tank. How fast its axis turns.
Even the wall counts. In VKS simulations, changing only its magnetic condition raised the threshold by about 40 percent.

Every turbulent dynamo simulation in three dimensions is very costly, so only a handful of knob settings get simulated. Each one is a mountain of data. A single snapshot can weigh more than a gigabyte.
Each run holds only a few flips, and between the dots, there is nothing at all.
Those gaps are where this film lives. The study behind this film asks three things.

1. Can a machine learn the whole family of fields, even at knob settings between the dots? 2. Can it respect each law where it holds, exactly in every field, or on average over many fields? 3. Can it tell us how often the field flips?
To find out, the study's plan climbs a staircase from three numbers to the shapes of real experiments.
One honest note, this independent study is prospective, built on small experiments on an ordinary computer and not endorsed by Milady, its partners or the supervisors.
An equation, windows, a panel of knobs, a handful of dots. Full simulations cost too much, so we start with a three-dial caricature that already flips. Can anyone say when it flips next?
With only a handful of runs, should the settings be spread evenly or packed near each threshold?

Here is the caricature. Three dials linked by springs. One is the dipole, the north-south part of the field. One is the quadrupole, a four-pole part. The third is a flow pattern driven by a knob, gamma.
Three short equations from G-Zan J tie them together. Flip both field dials and the equations read the same. Three dials, three numbers, the bottom step of the staircase.

Use two dials as a map. Quadrupole across, dipole up. With the knob low, the state circles in one whirlpool and stays. A mirror twin circles the mirror whirlpool, dipole down. Each start is trapped. The dipole never changes sign.

Now turn gamma up. Just above 0.86, the whirlpool's touch. A narrow corridor opens. The state lingers on one side, then slips through. The dipole flips. Nothing here is random. So, will the flips come like clockwork?
No. Long waits and short ones, irregularly. The dipole sign prints uneven stripes, like the seafloor.
Now count. One tick each time the dipole crosses zero. Not every tick is a flip. An excursion can cross and come straight back. Ticks per unit of time. The crossing rate.
Up to 0.86, silence. Just above, about two ticks per thousand time units. At gamma equal to 1, about 11.
Set gamma at 0.9 and launch two copies one millionth apart. We know the state to six decimals. Can we predict the date of the next flip?
At first, the copies move as one, but their gap nearly triples every 11 time units. After about 150, they disagree completely.
The average weight between crossings is longer, over 200. Each extra decimal buys only about 25 more time units, so the forecast fades before the average weight ends. Only the statistics survive.
The path is lost, so leave the shutter open. Each pass leaves a little light, a glow builds. A copy started on the other side first paints the mirror image. Given time, both paint the same glow.
Where does the dipole spend its time? Two humps, the same for both. This reproducible glow is the stationary distribution. Below the threshold, each start paints its own whirlpool.

Now film the trajectory. One frame every two time units. Neighboring frames look alike. Cut the film into frames. Drop them in a shoe box. Shake and throw away the timestamps. Pour the box out. The frames redraw the same glow.

Each frame is a snapshot, three dial readings, nothing more. It carries no time stamp and no time order. Yet the shoebox, plus the equations, answers many questions. Averages, energy budgets, even how often the dipole crosses zero.
Pick one photo. Its three dial readings give its energy. From that photo alone, the equations tell how fast its energy changes. Drop one marble per photo at that value.
Some photos are gaining energy, others losing it. The pile spreads wide, yet its average sits at zero. Energy in equals energy out on average.
Like a bank account, over the years income matches spending, yet each day gains or loses. This is a law of the crowd. It holds for the shoebox, not for each photo.
How many independent snapshots does each setting need, and how far apart must they be saved?
A puzzle. How many cars cross this line each hour? No clock, just one photo from above, where every speedometer can be read.
Can one photo, with no time in it, give you a rate?
It can. Draw a thin strip around the line. A fast car spends little time inside, so catching one there counts for more.
Add up the speeds of the cars inside and divide by the strip's width. On average, that is how many cars cross per hour.
Back to the shoebox. Spread its photos out by their dipole reading. The line to cross is zero. Draw a thin strip around it.
Each photo also needs a speedometer. No clock required. The dipole's equation turns the photo's three dial readings into a speed. Up or down, both count, so keep only its size.

Add the speeds inside the strip, then divide by its width and by the total number of photos. Out comes the crossing rate. Shrink the strip to nothing. And for well-behaved systems, the recipe is exact, Rice's formula. The catch, few photos land in a thin strip. Here, about two dozen out of 8,000. end.
Now test it against the truth. At 41 settings of gamma, long simulations count the crossings as they happen. Rice gets only the true snapshots, shuffled, plus the equations.

The two curves almost coincide. Shade the gap and divide by the area under the counted curve. The cumulative error, 4% near the threshold, 6% above it. A good sign on three chaotic dials that are not even guaranteed to be well behaved.

One caution. Rice counts crossings, not reversals. An excursion across zero and back adds two crossings, but no reversal. To isolate reversals, the PhD plan counts crossings of a far level on the other side.

So Rice needs only snapshots and the equations, but plenty of snapshots and cheap ones. Yet real dynamo simulations exist at only a few knob settings. Between the dots, there is no shoebox at all. How do you get snapshots at a setting nobody simulated?
For VKS, which dipole should rice count and what threshold turns a crossing into a reversal?
New snapshots start as pure noise, a round cloud of random points. Over it, the crowd we want, one point per snapshot. Here, two mirror blobs, like the two whirlpools.
Now let a wind blow through the cloud. Each point drifts, bends, and lands inside the shape of the data. Fresh noise in, fresh snapshots out, as many as you like.
That wind is a generative model. New, plausible examples, on demand. The whole game is learning the wind.
One warning before the formulas, the wind runs on its own transport clock from zero to one, not physical time. At the end, you hold one snapshot, not a movie.
and the wind's arrows move snapshots, not fluid. They are not the fluid's velocity.

How is the wind learned? With a simple trick. Keep one coordinate of each point and lay the transport clock out to the right. Pair each noise point with a random snapshot. Join them with a straight string. Thousands of strings crossing everywhere.

Pick one place at one moment. Several strings pass through, pointing different ways. The network learns one arrow there, their average direction. That is the whole training. Plain regression, like fitting a curve through points.
Follow the averaged wind, not the strings. The paths bend and drawn against the clock, they never cross. Learn the average exactly and the noise lands exactly on the data's crowd. out.
Now give the wind a knob. Turn it. The target changes shape and the cloud follows. One network, every setting.

On the three dials, a real network trained at the filled dots. It was tested at the open dots, never seen in training. In between, no theorem promises success, only tests can tell. Beyond the range, nothing was tested.
At an open dot, the network snapshots join the shoebox beside simulated ones.

A generated snapshot has no true twin, so we compare crowds. Picture each crowd as a pile of sand. A distribution distance scores how different the two piles are. The earth mover kind counts how much sand must move and how far.
A perfect model scored against the data. Will it get zero?

No, roll a fair die a thousand times, then a thousand more. Same die, same truth, yet the two histograms differ. That gap is the noise floor, about what a perfect model scores. Judge every model against it, at equal sample size, never against zero.
One catch, the samples must be independent. Overlap them and the floor drops too low as the report warns.
Which statistics must the generated fields match and how close to the noise floor counts as success?
Physics hands the machine two kinds of laws. Some hold for every single snapshot. Others hold only for the crowd. Two shelves, still empty.
Back to the three dials. At a gamma never seen in training. Gray, true snapshots. Violet, a plane generator. The shape is right.

Now weigh the sides. The truth is balanced. The machine is not. Only about four in ten of its snapshots point up. It copied its data. Below the threshold, each run stays in one whirlpool, and the runs split unevenly.

Two ways to teach the mirror. The first student, Data Augmentation, sees each training snapshot flipped half the time. The second, Equivariance, has the mirror built into its wind. A mirrored noise point always lands on the mirrored snapshot.
At a gamma neither has seen. Who stays balanced?

The built-in mirror. The first student tilts a little. Yet in the mirror's crowd, each snapshot still points one way. The mirror balances the crowd, not each snapshot. Its card goes on the crowd's shelf. Built-in, exactly.

Here is that tilt, setting by setting. Below the threshold, runs often split unevenly. At 0.86, only five of 16 runs point up. The plane machine copies the imbalance and spills it onto unseen settings.

Augmentation sits on the noise floor at its training settings. Between them, it drifts. The network fills the gaps freely. The built-in mirror stays on the floor everywhere. Flipped copies teach the mirror only where there are data.

Can the energy budget catch the tilt? No. Each whirlpool balances its own budget, so a mix of the two passes in any proportion. On a check of crowd laws, the most lopsided machine even edges ahead. The mirror needs its own tool.
Remember the budget of the shoebox. Snapshot by snapshot, energy rises or falls. Only the crowd balances, on average, like a bank account over the years.
Now, a tempting fix for the machine, force every generated snapshot to balance its budget exactly, better or worse.
Worse. Push each snapshot until its energy stops changing. The wide pile collapses into a spike at zero. A ledger where every single day balances. No real account looks like that.

The distribution distance to the truth grows nine-fold. A short proof says why. Even a perfect generator forced this way cannot match the truth. So the budget goes on the crowd shelf. On the next test bench, a cruder score is fooled by such a spike.

Impose the budget on the crowd during training. Draw a batch of snapshots at any gamma, even without data. Average their energy change and square it. This penalty, the crowd loss, vanishes only when the crowd balances.

But there is a trap. Even for a balanced crowd, a batch's average wobbles. Its square grows with the scatter. So training also squeezes the scatter, nudging every snapshot toward balance, toward the spike. It showed up while building this experiment. treatment.
The fix. Split the batch into two independent juries and multiply their averages. On average, the scatter drops out, leaving only the crowd's imbalance. Does it pay off? The next tests will tell.
In three dimensions, which budgets should generated fields meet on average, and must their spread match too?
New test bench. Whole fields, not three dials. A flat square of conducting fluid, its edges wrapping around. In blue, the swirl of the flow. In vermilion, the electric currents behind the field.
One knob, eta, how fast the field smudges. But a flat world cannot sustain a dynamo. Here, a random forcing keeps the field alive, a training ground for laws, not a dynamo.
Every training field passes the box test. It is divergence-free. Train a plane generator on them.
Will its fields be divergence-free?
No. Now lines appear and vanish inside the box. Relative to the field's own variations, the divergence is 0.41, a defect of order 1.
A soft penalty only lowers it to 0.34 for the flow, 0.16 for the field, and the magnetic energy comes out 2.7 times too high. This law belongs on the shelf for every snapshot.

First fix, draw a hill map, not arrows, and let the flow run along its contour lines. Where the lines crowd, it runs faster, so nothing piles up or leaks, whatever the landscape. The box agrees. Lines in, lines out.
So the machine draws two hill maps for the flow and the field. Zero divergence by construction, however badly it is trained.
Second fix, for any field, split it into swirl plus slope and delete the slope. Wave by wave, remove the part of each arrow along the wave's own direction.
The gauges fall to rounding error, down to 10 to the minus 17. Measured though, with the very operator used to enforce it.

Back to the plane generator. Why does it miss trained on clean data? Follow the part of a field breaking the law. To bring it exactly to zero, the wind must act as a spring that turns infinitely stiff as the transport clock runs out.
A bounded network cannot, and a sampler with finite steps cannot follow either. A gap of order 1 remains. Almost is not exactly.
Now the crowd law. On average, energy in equals energy out. Three ways to impose it, at settings of ADA never seen.
1. During training, the crowd loss with its two juries. Against a control run of equal length, the distribution distance drops from 2.5 to 0.7. The control itself gains nothing.
2. After training, reweight the generated crowd. Where the model is worst, a pole of 500 shrinks to one person, and the crowd gets worse.

Three, rescale every snapshot onto the budget. Each snapshot now dissipates the same, a spike under a thousandth of the true spread. Yet the same distribution distance built on spectra improves. It is fooled. Only the spread gives the spike away. The crowd loss shows no spike. week.
One training seat each. Interpolation only. Every model far above the noise floor.
Back to the two shelves, now full. For every snapshot, zero divergence. Build it in or project, and it holds exactly. A penalty only roughly.
For the crowd, the energy budget. Impose it on the crowd during training. Rewaiting afterwards fails where the model is poor. Forcing it onto each snapshot makes a spike.
And the mirror? Each snapshot is lopsided, so it is a crowd law, yet a network can carry it exactly, built in.
One rule sorts them all. Enforce each law where it is true.

Put the pieces together, the machine this study proposes. A wind carries noise to a symmetric crowd of codes, mirror built in. A decoder turns each code into hill maps, so every field is divergence free. And the energy budget is imposed on the crowd.
It has not been built as a whole. The experiments tested pieces on three dials and a flat sheet with small networks on an ordinary processor.
One question remains. From Snapshots, how well can we answer how often?
In the partners' solver snapshots, which laws hold exactly, and under which discrete operator?
And aside, the five statements behind the pictures, each is elementary. What matters is its exact scope.
The first is almost too simple. Suppose every field a decoder can draw obeys a linear law, like zero divergence. Then every sample obeys it, whatever the crowd of codes, however badly trained.
The proof is one line. The work is in the decoder. Hill maps in two dimensions, a vector potential in three, with its gauge fixed.

Second, the spring in full. If the data lie in a flat subspace, the ideal wind splits in two. Along it, a part a network can learn. Across it, a pull back, the stray part divided by the time left on the clock.
Followed exactly, that pull lands every sample in the subspace. Trained perfectly, the plane generator, both projections and hill maps, give the same crowd.
Cap the pull, and an order one stray part survives. Now add a small bounded error to the exact pull. Does a stray part survive?
No, the pull erases it, so the plane generator 0.41 reads as a missing pull, not a small error.
and the projected flow's tiny residue, single precision.
Third, penalties. A common one tests the model's guess of where its path will end. With the ideal wind, that guess averages the data that could lie ahead.
For a linear law, an average of lawful fields is lawful. The penalty vanishes at the optimum and moves nothing. Off the optimum, in a real network, it holds the law only roughly.
For a curved law, that fails. Two points on a circle average to a point inside. This is the Jensen gap. Now the penalty biases the optimum itself.
Fourth, the mirror, as a theorem. Make the wind equivariant, mirror a point, and its arrow mirrors too. Start from noise that looks the same in the mirror.
Then, every path has a mirror twin, so the generated crowd is exactly symmetric at every knob setting, even with lopsided or missing data.
If every true crowd is symmetric, averaging a wind with its mirror never raises the expected loss. The cost? Two network passes instead of one.

In the VKS cylinder, a half -turn swapping the two impellers is a second symmetry. If their speeds differ, it also flips the sign of that difference, the forcing asymmetry. The same proof covers it, untested so far.
Last, crowd laws. The equations give any quantity a rate of change at each snapshot. If the crowd is stationary, that rate averages to zero. For every quantity, the energy budget is one case.
The proof? Let every snapshot run for a moment. The crowd looks the same, so no average moves. The mean rate is zero.
Necessary, not sufficient. A crowd parked on an unstable fixed point passes every such test, so does an unstable loop. The fit to data must therefore stay in the loss.
Can we simulate only one sign of forcing asymmetry and let the impeller swap supply the other?
Earlier, a distribution distance meant moving sand. The experiments mainly use a cousin, built from pairs. Each dot is a snapshot.
average every distance across the two crowds, and double it. Subtract the average distance within each crowd. Zero means the same law.
Re-weighting up close, the model's crowd misses its target average. Leave every snapshot in place. Change only how much each counts.
Many weightings hit the target. The least distorting one is an exponential tilt, known as the eye projection.

Picture crowds as points. Those with the right average lie on a line. The tilted crowd is the foot of the perpendicular. Any other fix pays the tilt's cost, plus an extra, as in Pythagoras. And nothing moves. The tilted crowd lives only where the model's crowd was.
How much is left of a re-weighted crowd? Its effective sample size says, equal weights, the whole crowd. One giant weight, one person.
On the flat sheet, at the smallest test eta, the pole keeps 99%. At the three largest, it bottoms out. One snapshot in 500.
Rank the values by how far the model's budget was off. The pole shrinks in nearly the same order. Where the pole survives, little needed fixing. Where much needed fixing, it collapses.
On the three dials too, re-weighting improved no crowd. One snapshot weighed 33 times the average.
Picture a model that never visits the bridge between the two polarities, where every crossing happens.
Can re-weighting bring back the crossing rate?
No. Rice reads the rate inside the strip, and the strip is empty. Zero times any weight is zero. Push harder, and the weight piles onto a few snapshots at the edge.
Rewaiting cannot visit places the model never went. The Ph.D. plan's risk table agrees. Rewaiting alone is no fallback.
One test, eta at a time. At the largest, the base model's snapshots dissipate, on average, over twice the energy fed in. The crowd loss cuts the distribution distance from 7.7 to 2.2.
At the smallest, already good. No change. The control run stays put.
Same values where the poll collapsed. Training moved the crowd. Weights could not. One seed though.
If the crowd loss fails, what is the fallback, since re-weighting fails where the model is poor?

The toll counter is back. Every car is now generated. They come from the machine with the built-in mirror, 20,000 at each of 41 settings of gamma, most unseen in training. Rice, with the equations, turns them into a crossing rate.

Against the counted truth, far from the threshold, the cumulative error is 14 percent. Setting by setting, the miss averages 17 percent and reaches 65 percent at two settings. Near the threshold, the error climbs to 42 percent.

One model, one training seed. Rice needs the equations and gives a rate, not waiting times. So, the study's third question. Can a machine tell us how often? For crossings on three dials, far from the threshold, roughly yes. Near it, not yet.
Zoom in. The truth is silent, up to 0.86, but the machine changes smoothly with gamma.
Will its crossing rates switch on early, late, or on time?

early and late, but never on time. Below the threshold, it leaks false crossings, up to a tenth of the rate just above. At 0.865, it is late, less than a sixth of the counted rate. Just above, it overshoots, five crossings per thousand time units against 3.4.
Why? Picture the machine as a stiff sheet. As gamma turns, its crowd changes only so fast. The truth climbs a steep ramp. Just above 0.86, the corridor opens.
The sheet rounds the corner, too early, then too low. The data show both, early strays in the corridor, then too few at the threshold.
A theorem. At a true jump, a smooth machine misses by at least half of it, unless it is very supple or told which state the system is in.
Here, a ramp, not a jump, and one seed, consistent with the theorem, not proof. Nor does the theorem explain the overshoot.

The crowd loss on three dials at unseen settings. On the good machine, it halves the crowd law residuals, even for laws it never enforced. But the spread of energy changes shrinks by a quarter, a faint echo of the spike.
On a deliberately biased machine, it fails. One run diverged, the other got worse. On the crossing rate, with one seed, slightly better near the threshold, worse far from it.

Now the strictest judge, the noise floor. On three dials, the best machine sits at about twice its floor, but three numbers are easy. On the flat sheet of plasma, every model's spectrum miss far more than two data samples differ. At best, six-fold.
Two seeds on the dials, one on the sheet. The PhD plan asks for at least three. Every test sits between trained settings.

The scoreboard, eight mechanisms, each with a verdict. For every snapshot, hill maps and projection, exact. The penalty, approximate. For the crowd, the mirror, exact. The crowd loss, useful but not clean. The rest, failures.

Back to the study's three questions. One, between the dots, the shapes come out right, but no model reaches its noise floor. Two, each law where it holds, exactly yes, on average partly. Three, how often? Roughly right, far from the threshold, poor near it.
Three lessons, exact laws, build them in, crowd laws, impose them on the crowd, never on each snapshot, and judge every result against the noise floor with enough seeds.
Which settings should get runs long enough to count reversals, so a predicted rate can be checked.

How wide should Rice's strip be? Widen it. The estimate blurs, its bias growing like the width squared. Narrow it. The estimate jitters as fewer snapshots land inside. The three-dial experiment used snapshots within 0.2 of zero.
With endless snapshots, why not shrink it to nothing? The exact formula assumes a smooth cloud. A cosine has only a thin ring, yet the formula still finds two crossings per period.
Chaos may lack a smooth cloud too, so nothing guarantees the limit. On the three dials, the only test so far, the answer depends on the strip.

To count reversals, not crossings, raise the bar. A reversal must run from above some level to below its mirror image. So the level's crossing rate, which Rice reads from snapshots, caps the reversal rate.
Wobbles across the level loosen the cap. The conjecture. If a flip lasts far longer than a wobble, the cap is nearly exact on a plateau of levels.
The bet, written before the data, from the PhD plan. On the staircase's first step, the cap comes within 30% of the counted rate on that plateau.
Confidence, medium. The cap is proved, the plateau is not. Ask first, how wide must that plateau be?
One more limit. Approved one. These two smooth random signals share one snapshot law. Value and speed alike. Same rice rate. Yet one crosses zero like a metronome. The other at uneven gaps.
On three dials, Zisanger found a shape in the weights between flips, a comb of short, quantized weights, then a memoryless exponential tail.
No shoebox holds that shape, it takes the movie. The open question, can short runs launched from generated states in the corridor supply the weights?
The staircase's first step gets a second round. Three seeds, not two. A second model, distilled from VKS simulations. And the impeller swap mirror, which also flips gamma.
Four lamps must light, lopsidedness, unenforced laws, rice, the level bound.

The bet. Unenforced residuals have again, roughly. Last time, having meant 1.98 against a bar of 2. A toss-up. Confidence? Medium. One catch. A perfectly symmetric model lands above the noise floor nearly half the time. The floor is its average. Ask first. Should the first lamp use a statistical test?
Beyond how often, for VKS, should we also target waiting times with short solver runs from generated states?
So far, every test ran on toy models. Before real dynamos, back to the map of the field, zoom into its thin, data-driven lane. It opens into four tracks.
A laboratory dynamo sets every track four tests, three dimensions, walls with iron and a vacuum, a tiny magnetic Prandtl number, and rare flips.

First track. Fast surrogates. Networks trained to imitate a solver. Some carry the equations in their loss. Others learn maps between whole fields. For conducting fluids, they now reach flat, two-dimensional turbulence. For the Earth, recall the 2022 study. The methods it tried could not reliably foresee a flip.
Their weak spot, trained to minimize a mean square error, ensembles of them regress to the mean flow. A cloud with two polarities collapses to its middle.

Second track, generative models, which learn the whole cloud, not just its middle. Adversarial networks first, then diffusion, then flow matching, the family the study used. They now dream three-dimensional turbulence, global weather ensembles, and steady turbulent states for chosen settings.
Trained on dynamo simulations? We found none.

Third track, making samples obey the laws. Four families. Hard. Build the law into the network, say a potential whose curl has no divergence, or project each sample while drawing it. Soft. A penalty in the loss, obeyed only approximately. On the distribution, constrain the crowd cloud, by its covariance, or by the equation a steady cloud obeys. And symmetry, an equivariant flow, gives a symmetric cloud.

A 2026 preprint compared ways to impose zero divergence on flat flows. No single strategy dominates. In three dimensions, we found two exactly divergence-free generators, both preprints, periodic box turbulence, and a current free field in the sun's corona. None handles walls, a vacuum outside and iron inside.

Fourth track, data assimilation, merging a model with a few measurements. Learned priors came in through compressed latent spaces, then diffusion models, and the library now plugs deep networks into Kalman filters and variational methods.
We found no diffusion prior used this way for conducting fluids. Near a flip, the answer has two polarities, and a prior that ignores the mirror could bias it toward one.

Now the rings. Papers cosigned by the supervisors. Dynamo side. Taylor Green dynamos pushed to small magnetic prantle numbers, and the VKS tank with its iron impellers simulated in two codes. In 2026, both codes produced VKS reversals, and a four-dial model reproduces their main features. Learning side. Auto encoder latent spaces read through classical flow modes, von Karman flow included, and assimilation and diffusion models built on deep networks outside conducting fluids.
Three ingredients are in hand, but in what we found, none of the four has published a generative model trained on dynamo data.
Where the generative and constraint tracks cross the dynamo tracks, we found the map empty. An independent thesis proposal aims at that spot. Five gaps, each beside its nearest neighbor.

1. A generator of dynamo fields 2. Velocity and magnetic field with exactly zero divergence in a walled cylinder with iron and vacuum 3. Energy budgets imposed on the distribution with no target value, even where there are no data 4. The flip rate read from snapshots with Rice's formula 5. One generator that crosses the dynamo threshold.
The study tested pieces on toy cases, exact potentials on a flat sheet, a budget imposed without data, Rice's formula on three dials.

The field moves fast. A 2026 conference paper claims to be the first to recognize a trade-off between physical and distributional accuracy. The study's lesson, never force a crowd law on each snapshot, must be placed against it.

Not claimed. Waiting times between flips. Sodium's tiny magnetic Prandtl number. The Earth's core. Real laboratory data. Each empty spot is a search result, not a proof, to be checked again before every paper.
First, VKS data. Should the generator train on the LaTU periodic grid or the S -Femin cylinder mesh?
Back to the staircase. The first two steps are lit by small experiments. Three numbers, then a flat sheet. The third, the twisting box, has only a preview.
From there up, every step is a bet, written down before the data exists in an independent PhD proposal.

To climb, the study first built a factory for the data. A recipe card sets the knobs. Ovens run one simulation per setting, on a laptop or a cluster. Each result is sealed in a labeled jar, a unique number, the code version, a checksum.
A ledger records every jar, a menu splits them for training and testing, the chef learns, and a critic scores the result.
It all runs end-to-end on an ordinary processor, never yet on a graphics card or a real cluster. A gray tag names the file. Each empty frame awaits.
First product off the line. The flat sheet. 11 diffusivities. 16 runs each. The bet. A check on the data. At every setting, the average dissipation matches the injected power within 5%.

Open one oven. The solver keeps flow and field as waves, where a curl is a multiplication. Products are easier on the grid. Each step hops over and back. It trims the outer third of the waves, so products cannot fold back as fakes. A projection keeps both fields divergence-free. The smudging is solved exactly. quickly.
One step at 64 cubed, eight hundredths of a second, on an ordinary processor. The memory peak, about 15 times the state, is an estimated 6 gigabytes at 256 cubed.

Open one jar, one simulation, one file, laid out like the well, a reference dataset for machine learning. Inside, the velocity and the magnetic field, snapshot after snapshot, and time series of energies and divergences. The file carries a unique identifier and the codes commit.
The catalog repeats that identifier and adds a checksum so an offline cluster can rebuild its rows from the files alone. Checksummed, not sealed. A forced rewrite updates the checksum.

Follow one campaign down the line. One command reads the recipe, the flat sheet, 11 diffusivities. The launcher opens one task per setting. Each integrates 16 runs side by side and writes one file. Each task adds a ledger row, its status, checksum, and wall time. time.

This campaign has not run yet. The BET, all 11 tasks finish, each with a checksummed file. Confidence is high, small test campaigns already finished in seconds. The report's own data from the same solver took about half an hour.
A new instrument for the critic. In the flat sheet, field lines are contours of one potential. Lines loop around O points and cross at X points. On this periodic square, which kind is more common?
Neither. Exactly as many of each. A free check on any counter.
The internship offer asks for topology. The report computed none. A low-confidence bet. Generated fields match the simulated count. The plan lists the count, but sets no pass mark.
Which topology metric should judge generated fields and what gap in x-point counts fails a model?

Before trusting the solver, test it on a known answer. The twisting flow offers one, a field shaped exactly like it. Its lines follow the flow's own lines, so carrying and stretching cancel. Only diffusion acts. Its growth rate is exactly minus one over Rm.
So the measured rate, the slowest fade, can be no lower, at Rm2 minus one -half. The solver finds minus 0 .5001 on the bound to about one part in 10 ,000.
Run long enough and one field takes over, the slowest to fade or the fastest to grow. The surface wraps its strong parts, threads trace its lines.

At RM8, it fades. At 12 and 16, inside the window, it grows. At 20, just past it, it fades again. In these snapshots, at 8, 16, and 20, it gathers in four slim tubes. They peek at points where the flow stands still. At 12, it spreads out.
Published work described such cigar-shaped tubes and symmetries the report did not check. One shape per setting. Proposed first targets for a three-dimensional generator.
How precise are those edges? Each run gets a long fit over its second half, a late fit over its last quarter, a finer grid rechecks two settings. At RM12, all three agree.
At 17 and a half, right on the edge. Same sign.

No, the long fit says growing, the late fit and finer grid fading. This edge is known to about 0.1, the third near 27 to about 1. A likely cause still unchecked, the modes oscillate, so the growth curve wobbles. The divergence, at least, stays at rounding error. That unresolved sign is where Bet One begins.
Near the thresholds, should we fit growth rates with an oscillation term or simply run longer?
Bet one, the twisting box. At 32 cubed, the small sweep matched the published windows. But near 17 and a half, the sign of growth stayed unresolved.

The campaign doubles the resolution and steps RM by whole numbers up to 40. The bet? Growth still positive at 17, already negative at 18, with two fits agreeing, one over the kept part of the run, one over its last quarter.
Confidence, medium. At 18, the small sweep's two fits already differed by more than the rate itself. Worth asking before the run. Add three points between 17 and 18.
Bet 2, the first true dynamo, a Taylor green flow of counter-rotating eddies. Now the field pushes back on the flow. Above a threshold, a tiny seed should grow, then level off.
12 runs cross 4 Reynolds numbers with 3 values of Pm. The bet? A threshold in Rm, bracketed for at least 2 values of Pm.

Confidence, medium. Published runs define the Reynolds number differently, so the threshold may fall off this grid. Near threshold, a run may still be growing when its snapshots are kept. Lengthen those runs, or flag and exclude them.
Near a gentle threshold, the truth rises like a square root, vertical at first. A stiff machine rounds the corner. A supple one airs less, but turns jumpy everywhere.
Near a subcritical threshold, two states coexist. In published Taylor Green runs, a dynamo, once on, survived down to a third of its threshold. Told only the knob, a machine blends them.
The plans bet. Tell it the branch, and its threshold error at least halves.
Confidence, low. Statistical stability along branches is unproven in turbulence. No downward sweep is configured, from which saturated runs, and how far down.

Some things need no bet. In three dimensions, hill maps become potentials. The generator draws them, then takes their curl. So the flow in the field stay divergence-free to rounding, even with untrained weights.
Mirror the starting noise, and the sample comes out with its field flipped. That shows the mechanism, not the quality.
Everything else must be measured. First test, does the generator get the energy spectra right within a tenth of a decade at the settings it trained on?
confidence low. In two dimensions, the best models only just got there, and here each run keeps 40 snapshots against 5,000 in the plan.
Now the crowd law in three dimensions. Energy in equals energy out, on average. In two dimensions, the crowd loss cut the budget error to 6 percent. An equal length control run stayed at 46.
The bet. Under 5% at held out settings. The control higher, the dissipation spread within a fifth.
Confidence? Low. On three dials, the loss shrank the spread of energy changes and failed from a biased start. Ask first, where runs may still be growing, trust the data or the crowd law.
before the Taylor Green runs, which forcing Reynolds number definition and resolution make their threshold comparable with published ones.
Two steps remain. The VKS cylinder with its iron impellers and dress dine, a precessing cylinder. First, what exact means once there are walls, metals, and meshes? Then there bets.
Before the walls, one convention. In the sodium experiment, Rm has no single definition. One paper multiplies by an impeller efficiency near 0.6. Another does not. A third uses other radii.
so one threshold reads about 31 or 52 to 71. A generator conditioned on RM must say which it means.
Now the walls. Many potentials draw the same field. Add the slope of any hill and the curl is unchanged. Choose among them without a fixed rule and the generator learns noise.

So fix the gauge. No divergence inside, no potential flowing through the wall. A published theorem then gives each admissible field one potential, none lost, none counted twice. If the field never crosses the wall, the potential may instead meet it at right angles.
One metric changes meaning, where the field crosses the wall. Magnetic helicity depends on the gauge, so a relative helicity is needed.
Now the iron that made VKS work. At its surface, the part of the field crossing it is continuous, and so is the part along it, divided by the permeability.
Can a smooth potential obey both rules?
No. A smooth potential keeps the field continuous, breaking the second rule unless the field meets the iron head-on. The plan proposes an untested fix, a potential deliberately kinked at the surface.
Outside, the field must join a current free field, linear but non-local, each wall point depending on the whole wall. How to impose it is open.
In the periodic box, two scalars—palloidal and toroidal— can replace a potential's three components. Their field is divergence-free, with no gauge. The plan stores its box data that way.
The partner solver slices space instead. Around the axis, waves of zero, one, two, three bumps per turn. Across each half plane, a triangle mesh.

A continuous potential on that mesh gives a divergence-free curl, wave by wave. But the solver's data are only nearly divergence-free. The generator will be cleaner than its data. Measure with the solver's yardstick.
The VKS bet would train a generator on the partner simulations of the sodium experiment. In their reference run, four patterns dominate—a dipole, a quadrupole, and two flow patterns.

The BET, their energy shares within 10% and the distribution distance of dipole and quadrupole under twice the noise floor, plus the iron rule within 1% and Rice's reversal rate inside the simulated counts error bars.
Confidence, low. The data are not public, no file reader exists yet, and few reversals mean wide error bars. Worth asking first, how many snapshots per configuration and by when?
The dress -dyne bet. A sodium cylinder spinning while its axis slowly turns. Its knob, the precession ratio. How fast the axis turns relative to the spin.
The generator draws only the flow. A solver finds the threshold and the symmetry of the field that flow would grow. The bet? Both write at an unseen ratio. The threshold within 10 percent.
Confidence? Low. Few ratios are planned and this step would be dropped first. Worth asking now, how many ratios and how close together?
Downstream, the generator feeds reduced models. Their best drift averages the equation's drift over snapshots sharing a reduced state. No time series needed.
It also serves as a prior. A probe reads the dipole near zero, midreversal. Where does the average of the matching states sit?

between two mirror humps where the dynamo almost never is. Methods keeping only a mean and a spread chase that ghost. A lopsided prior would wrongly favor one hump. A built-in mirror handles it exactly. Sample mirror pairs or search from a code and its mirror.
Which labels must each VKS snapshot carry? Which RM definition? Which wall condition? Which iron permeability?

No graphics card hour has been measured yet. The bet? Measured costs land within a factor of two of the plan.

Back to the compass and to the two questions.

When will this needle turn? For the Earth, no one can say. In a simple computer model, chaos makes the forecast fade before the average weight ends. But how often the field flips, counted as crossings of zero, can still be answered. The answer hides in a shoebox of snapshots, read with the equations. And a machine can learn to dream such snapshots between the simulated settings.

On small test problems, it partly works. The mirror holds by construction at every setting. On three dials, the rate of zero crossings is roughly right far from the threshold and poor near it. A smooth machine rounds off a steep change. The bigger tests, in three dimensions and in the shapes of real machines, are written as bets.
One lesson remains. Enforce each law where it is true. Exactly where it is exact. On average, where it only holds on average.
The report, the code, and every result in this film are on the project's site, with their limits written out. The rest of the staircase is still to be computed.
Leave the periodic box for a real vessel, and exact gets harder. The potential needs a gauge and a wall condition. Then each field has exactly one.
At the soft iron impellers, field lines bend sharply at the iron surface, so a smooth potential cannot be exact. It needs a kink there.

Outside, the field must match a current free field in the vacuum. The rule is linear but non-local. The field at one point of the wall depends on the whole wall. Imposing it exactly and cheaply for every sample is still open.
The top steps are simulations of real machines, the VKS cylinder, and Dressed Dine, a precessing cylinder.

Their bets are already written. For VKS, the four main patterns with the right energy shares, and Rice's reversal rate inside the simulated counts error bars. For Dresden, the threshold at an unseen precession rate within 10%.
Those simulations belong to the project's partners, are not public, and must be requested.
